1    I.     Introduction.
2           1.      Advertised “sale” prices are important to consumers. Consumers are more likely to
3    purchase an item if they know that they are getting a good deal. Further, if consumers think that a
4    sale will end soon, they are likely to buy now, rather than wait, comparison shop, and buy
5    something else.
6           2.      While there is nothing wrong with a legitimate sale, a fake one—that is, one with
7    made-up regular prices, made-up discounts, and made-up expirations—is deceptive and illegal.
8           3.      Section 17500 of California’s False Advertising Law prohibits businesses from
9    making statements they know or should know to be untrue or misleading. Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §
10   17500. This includes statements falsely suggesting that a product is on sale, when it actually is not.
11          4.      Moreover, section 17501 of California’s False Advertising Law provides that “[n]o
12   price shall be advertised as a former price … unless the alleged former price was the prevailing
13   market price … within three months next immediately preceding” the advertising. Cal. Bus. &
14   Prof. Code § 17501. So, in addition to generally prohibiting untrue and misleading fake discounts,
15   it also specifically prohibits this particular flavor of fake discount (where the advertised former
16   price is not the prevailing price during the specified timeframe).
17          5.      In addition, California’s Consumer Legal Remedies Act prohibits “advertising goods
18   or services with the intent not to sell them as advertised” and specifically prohibits “false or
19   misleading statements of fact concerning reasons for, existence of, or amounts of price reductions.”
20   Cal. Civ. Code § 1770(a)(9), (13).
21          6.      Moreover, the Federal Trade Commission’s regulations prohibit false or misleading
22   “former price comparisons,” for example, making up “an artificial, inflated price … for the purpose
23   of enabling the subsequent offer of a large reduction” off that price. 16 C.F.R. § 233.1.
24          7.      So, as numerous courts have found, fake sales violate these laws. They also violate
25   California’s general prohibition on unlawful, unfair, and deceptive business practices. See Cal. Bus.
26   & Prof. Code § 17200.
27
28

3    Defendant’s website, www.mixbook.com.
4           9.       On its website, Defendant advertises discounts on everything or “almost everything”
5    it sells (the “Mixbook Products” or “Products”). 1 It lists purported regular prices and purported
6    limited-time sales offering steep discounts—for example, “up to 50% off”—from those listed

1           29.     For all these reasons, even on days where the promotion advertised on the homepage
2    requires a minimum purchase, all or nearly all of Defendant’s Products—including ones with a list
3    price below the minimum purchase threshold needed to qualify for the promotion advertised on the
4    homepage—are subject to a significant discount.
5           30.     To confirm that Defendant always offers discounts off purported regular prices,
6    Plaintiff’s counsel performed an investigation of Defendant’s advertising practices using the
7    Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine (available at www.archive.org). 4 That investigation confirms
8    that Defendant’s sales are always available. Counsel collected 58 randomly selected screenshots of
9    Defendant’s website, www.mixbook.com, from the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine, from
10   2023-2025. Counsel also collected screenshots directly from Defendant’s website in 2025 from 49
11   different days. A review of these screenshots confirmed that Defendant’s sales have persisted
12   continuously for years. On every single day for which counsel reviewed Defendant’s website,
13   Defendant advertised a sitewide discount.
14          31.     More specifically, the screenshots counsel collected show that Defendant was
15   running a sitewide sale that applied to everything or “almost everything” (i.e., to all Products), with
16   no minimum purchase, on 97 out of 107 days.
17          32.     On the remaining 10 days, the screenshot of the home page depicted a sitewide sale
18   requiring a minimum purchase, and no “Promo Terms” page showing what other promotions were
19   running at the time was available. For the reasons stated above, it is highly likely that, even on those
20   days, the vast majority, if not all, of Defendant’s Products were eligible for a promotion entitling the
21   purchaser to a substantial discount off the supposed list prices.
22          33.     Reasonable consumers do not realize the fake nature of Defendant’s promotions.
23   That Defendant’s sales are not real sales and instead persist indefinitely is not apparent from merely
24   purchasing the Products, because the sale appears to be a bona fide sale. Consumers do not have any
25   reason to go back to the website day after day to discover that there is still a sale. And, even a
26   consumer who occasionally checks the website would reasonably believe that there happened to be

2    which revealed that the sale is not limited in time, that the discounts are fake, and that the advertised
3    regular prices are fake.
4            34.        Some of Defendant’s purported sales purport to require consumers to apply a coupon
5    code to the order to get the discount. In at least some (and potentially all) cases, the codes are
6    automatically applied to the order, meaning that everyone who buys during the purported sale
7    received the discount. Regardless, the codes are advertised extensively throughout the website and
8    purport to offer substantial savings, so—even in circumstances where the code must be applied, if
9    any—the code is applied to substantially all or all orders placed on Defendant’s website.
10           35.        In addition to advertising fake limited time sales, Defendant’s website lists fake
11   regular prices (that is, prices reflecting the list price or value of an item) and fake purported savings
12   off those purported regular prices.
13           36.        For example, on August 20, 2025, Defendant advertised a purported limited-time
14   sale of up to 55% off. As part of this sale, Defendant listed purported regular prices in smaller,
15   black, strikethrough font along with the purported discounted price in larger, bold, orange font. In
16   this example, Defendant represented that a Square, 10x10, Matte Hardcover, Everyday Semi-Gloss,
17   30 page “Hardcover Photo Book” had a list price of $85.89 and a discounted price of $60.98 when
18   the “EXTRAGIFT” code was applied:

25   “Hardcover Photo Book” is not its regular price. Instead, the true regular price is much lower,
26   because Defendant always offers steep sitewide discounts on it. As a result, Defendant’s customers
27   who bought that Product did not receive $24.91 off. They received a much lower discount, or no
28   discount at all.

1            38.     Using these tactics, Defendant leads reasonable consumers to believe that they will
2    get a discount on the Products they are purchasing if they purchase during the limited-time
3    promotion. In other words, it leads reasonable consumers to believe that if they buy now, they will
4    get a Product worth X at a discounted, lower price Y. This creates a sense of urgency: buy now, and
5    you will receive something worth more than you pay for it; wait, and you will pay more for the
6    same thing later.
7            39.     Based on Defendant’s advertisements, reasonable consumers reasonably believe that
8    the list prices Defendant advertises are Defendant’s regular prices and former prices (that is, the
9    price at which the goods were actually offered for sale on Defendant’s website before the limited-
10   time offer went into effect). In other words, reasonable consumers reasonably believe that the list
11   prices Defendant advertises represent the amount that consumers formerly had to pay on
12   Defendant’s website for Defendant’s goods, before the limited-time sale began, and will again have
13   to pay for Defendant’s goods when the sale ends. Said differently, reasonable consumers
14   reasonably believe that, prior to the supposedly time-limited sale, consumers buying from
15   Defendant on its website had to pay the list price to get the item and did not have the opportunity to
16   get a discount from that list price.
17           40.     Reasonable consumers also reasonably believe that the list prices Defendant
18   advertises represent the true market value of the Products, and are the prevailing prices for those
19   Products; and that they are receiving reductions from those listed regular prices in the amounts
20   advertised. In truth, however, Defendant always offers discounts off the purported regular prices it
21   advertises. As a result, everything about Defendant’s price and purported discount advertising is
22   false. The list prices Defendant advertises are not actually Defendant’s regular or former prices, or
23   the prevailing prices for the Products Defendant sells. And, the list prices do not represent the true
24   market value for the Products, because Defendant’s Products are always available for less than that
25   on Defendant’s website, and customers did not have to formerly pay that amount to get those items.
26   The purported discounts Defendant advertises are not the true discount the customer is receiving,
27   and are often not a discount at all. Nor are the purported discounts limited-time—quite the opposite,
28   they are always available.

     Class Action Complaint                                11                     Case No. 3:25-cv-07142
              Case 3:25-cv-07142-VC          Document 1        Filed 08/22/25      Page 14 of 32




1           41.     Defendant’s purported regular prices were not the prevailing prices during the 90
2    days immediately preceding Defendant’s advertisement of the purported discounts. As explained
3    and shown above, Mixbook always offers discounts on its Products. As a result, for any 90-day
4    period, the most common, and prevailing, price of those Products are the supposedly discounted
5    prices that are always available on Defendant’s website, not the advertised list or regular prices.
6           B.      Defendant’s advertisements are unfair, deceptive, and unlawful.
7           42.     Section 17500 of California’s False Advertising Law prohibits businesses from
8    making statements they know or should know to be untrue or misleading. Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §
9    17500. This includes statements falsely suggesting that a product is on sale, when it actually is not.
10          43.     Moreover, section 17501 of California’s False Advertising Law specifically provides
11   that “[n]o price shall be advertised as a former price … unless the alleged former price was the
12   prevailing market price … within three months next immediately preceding” the advertising. Cal.
13   Bus. & Prof. Code § 17501.
14          44.     In addition, California’s Consumer Legal Remedies Act prohibits “advertising goods
15   or services with the intent not to sell them as advertised” and specifically prohibits “false or
16   misleading statements of fact concerning reasons for, existence of, or amounts of price reductions.”
17   Cal. Civ. Code § 1770(a)(9), (13).
18          45.     In addition, the Federal Trade Commission’s regulations prohibit false or misleading
19   “former price comparisons,” for example, making up “an artificial, inflated price … for the purpose
20   of enabling the subsequent offer of a large reduction” off that price. 16 C.F.R. § 233.1.
21          46.     And finally, California’s unfair competition law bans unlawful, unfair, and deceptive
22   business practices. See Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200.
